It's hard to tell exactly what you are modeling without seeing the full syntax.  The output shows that Loy is defined by Com and Rec, yet you describe Com as a second-order factor and Loy as a first-order factor, which might imply the opposite (i.e., if Com is a latent construct that is an indicator of Loy, then Loy must be a higher-order factor).

As far as the factor loading = 1 is concerned, the default setting in sem() is to identify the construct by fixing the first loading to 1, but you can override that in the syntax (e.g., Loy =~ NA*Com) or in the call to sem() by choosing a different method of identification: sem(model, data, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE).  Again, without seeing your full syntax, it's hard to see the problem.

Terry

categorical data (in lavaan 0.5-15). It was written at the time with

messages.subject_clean: Reliability questions on CFA
messages.body_plain:
Wanted to close the loop on this, as it just dawned on me that Fornell & Larcker's composite reliability and McDonald's Omega are the "same" (well, not really, Tenko Raykov pointed it out to me a while back and I never got around to thinking about it until now). Sorry if this is too basic for everyone - sometimes it takes me a while to realize simple things.

See the formula's laid out here:

F&L, equation 10: http://faculty-gsb.stanford.edu/larcker/PDF/6%20Unobservable%20Variables.pdf
Omega, equation 2 (page 6): http://mailer.fsu.edu/~akamata/papers/MD_rel_paper.pdf

The notation is slightly different, but the meaning is the same. The key for my simple brain to remember was the denominator for Omega is the sample variance-covariance matrix, which is the same as the squared loadings + residual variance, which is the denominator in F&L composite reliability.

You can get composite reliability to equal omega but you first have to make sure you are getting the freely estimated factor loadings, so you have to fix the factor variance to 1 or whatever. Then you simply follow F&L's formula, and it will give you Omega.

library(MASS)
library(lavaan)
library(psych)

#Generate 3 multivariate normal variables, with differing degrees of correlation.
Sigma<-matrix(c(1,.6,.3,
                .6,1,.4,
                .3,.4,1),3,3)
data<-as.data.frame(mvrnorm(n=1000,rep(0,3),Sigma))
colnames(data)<-c("x1","x2","x3")

#Specify and estimate a simple CFA model, fixing the variance to 1.
model<-"y=~NA*x1+x2+x3
        y~~1*y"
model_fit<-cfa(model,data=data)
summary(model_fit)

#extract from the results the residual variances and the loadings.
v<-diag(inspect(model_fit,"coef")$theta)
l<-inspect(model_fit,"coef")$lambda

#calculate composite reliability
cr<-sum(l)^2/(sum(l)^2+sum(v))

#Calculate omega
omega(data)$omega_h
#results differ slightly, probably due to differences in computation.

Now if you have a multidimensional construct, or you are doing more complicated paths between indicator variables, then it may not come out exactly as Omega in the psych package will get you. That's because Omega isn't really estimating your CFA - it's doing an EFA, some rotation, etc. (you can read the help file), so it won't give you the same thing. But I would argue that since you are really estimating a confirmatory model and you have delineated the relationships, that's the reliability you want to test, not the reliability that Omega as estimated by psych gives you.

If you do so, you will not be able to use FIML to account for missing data, so you might consider using multiple imputation.  The sem.mi() function in the semTools package automates the process of imputation, analysis, and pooling results.  If you are on the fence about whether 3-level ordinal variables should be treated as continuous, you can get some idea about the practical consequences by reading this article:  http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0029315

The paper on lavaan.survey, a package to do SEM with complex survey data (or just data with weights, clusters, and strata) is now out in today's issue of the Journal of Statistical Software. See here

Another example using multiple group modeling of ESS data is included in an upcoming (1 April) blog post created by Anthony D'Amico for his trove of R survey analyses: http://www.asdfree.com/ .

Enjoy!

Daniel

10 Using categorical variables

Binary, ordinal and nominal variables are considered categorical (not continuous). It makes a big di

these categorical variables are exogenous (independent) or endogenous (dependent) in the model.

Exogenous categorical variables
If you have a binary exogenous covariate (say, gender), all you need to

an exogenous ordinal variable, you can use a coding scheme reecting the order (say, 1,2,3,. . . ) and treat it

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am encountering some problems when evaluating a model that includes a composite variable and to which I added replicate weights (because my data points do not have an equal accuracy).

My model includes a quadratic and linear effect of rainfall on some endogenous variables. To test the combined effect of rainfall on the other variables, I want to add a composite variable.

The model without composite variable looks like this:

modeldiam <- '
Sqrt.AGB_Ch_10cm ~ SP50stem_10cm + diam_mean_10cm + T_CEC_SOIL + Prec.m + Prec.m.squared
SP50stem_10cm ~ T_CEC_SOIL + Prec.m  + Prec.m.squared
diam_mean_10cm ~ T_CEC_SOIL +  Prec.m
'
fitdiam <- sem(modeldiam, estimator="ML", fixed.x=T, data=averdata.all.unique)

survey.design <- svydesign (id=~1, , weights = ~Weight, data=averdata.all.unique) # This is including replicate weights
fit.totaldiam <- lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit=fitdiam, survey.design=survey.design, estimator = "MLM")  # This evaluates the model taking into account the replicate weights
summary(fit.totaldiam, standardized=T, fit.measures=T)

This model works well.

Then, when adding a composite variable for the combined effect of rainfall, the model looks like this:

modelcomposite1 <- '
Rainfall <~ 10.314*Prec.m + Prec.m.squared
Sqrt.AGB_Ch_10cm ~ Rainfall + T_CEC_SOIL + SP50stem_10cm + diam_mean_10cm
SP50stem_10cm ~ T_CEC_SOIL + Rainfall
diam_mean_10cm ~ T_CEC_SOIL + Prec.m
'

fitcomposite <- sem(modelcomposite1, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, data=averdata.all.unique)

Until here, it works fine as well. But when including the replicate weights, the problem starts:

fit.totalcomposite <- lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit=fitcomposite, survey.design=survey.design, estimator = "MLM")

Warning message:

In lavaan::lavaan(model = modelcomposite1, model.type = "sem", int.ov.free = TRUE,  :

  lavaan WARNING: model has NOT converged!

Even when I try to reduce the model (e.g., take out 1 or 2 variables or paths), the problem remains. Does anyone know why this could be the case??

I would be grateful for any help!

Regards,
Masha

messages.body_plain:
First of all cheers for providing the workable example. I had to make only minor changes to the R script to make it run fine.

A couple of comments about the initial model it produces. You notice all fit indices are not promising - RMSEA=0.1, CFI/TLI are under 0.9. You also have some items with low loadings: a6 loads under 0.3 on ct1. These are going to be signs that you have parameters that are not "correctly" specified. You'll notice the first 3 modindices all pertain to item a6, which has that low loading. The epc for the mod on dm, and negative for the mods on as and ct2.

Another interesting thing here is the correlation matrix of the factors (I say correlation because you've fixed the variances to 1 I believe), obtained via
inspect(fitcfa1,"coef")$psi

Obtains negative relationships between dm and ct2 and as. Right now a6 loads low on ct1, which has a positive correlation with dm, none with ct1, and positive with as. This correlation structure looks a little odd - and could be driven by the misplacement of a6.

Look what happens when you respecify the model following the modindices - make a6 load on ct2 and as. Fit stats are slightly better (though not drastically); a6 still loads low on the two other factors, so again you may want to adjust. Even consider removing entirely - if you try that, the fit stats actually improve slightly more. The largest modindices now don't have a6 in them. Run an EFA using factanal(data,factors=4) and you'll see that a6 doesn't load with a7 and a8.

You still have high modindices and poor fit, so you need to make further adjustments to your model. Keep in mind, though, once you start making tons of changes to your model, your theory gets called into question.

Not knowing anything about what you are modeling, here are some thoughts:
- Are you modeling ill-defined or relatively broad constructs? It could be that a small number of items per construct isn't enough to really establish that you are measuring anything.
- Are your items truly conceptually aligned? Maybe there is something missing among them?

In general I have found that modeling with categorical and dichotomous variables, because the variability is less, sometimes you have to do a lot more "thinking" about your model.

You certainly should be able to deal with both missing data and categorical indicators! In your script, you're missing the bit that tells lavaan which variables are categorical. At the end of the runMI command you can add any arguments you'd like passed to lavaan. In the case of categorical data you want to include the ordered argument with the names of the categorical variables. I've included an example of this below.

One other note, right now with categorical data the chi="Mplus" option will kick back an error (the only option for chi square combination is the lmrr method).

Hope this helps,

Alex

Example (adapted from the runMI documentation and simsem examples):
library(semTools)
library(lavaan)
library(mice)

popModel <- "
f1 =~ 0.6*y1 + 0.6*y2 + 0.6*y3 + 0.6*y4
y1 ~*~ 1*y1
y2 ~*~ 1*y2
y3 ~*~ 1*y3
y4 ~*~ 1*y4
f1 ~~ 1*f1
y1 | 0.5*t1
y2 | 0.25*t1
y3 | 0*t1
y4 | -0.5*t1
"

analyzeModel <- "
f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
 y1 ~*~ 1*y1
 y2 ~*~ 1*y2
 y3 ~*~ 1*y3
 y4 ~*~ 1*y4
"

dat <- simulateData(popModel, sample.nobs = 200L)
miss.pat <- matrix(as.logical(rbinom(prod(dim(dat)), 1, 0.2)), nrow(dat), ncol(dat))
dat[miss.pat] <- NA

datami <- mice(dat, m=5,seed=12345,method=c("pmm","pmm","pmm","pmm"))

mice.imp <- NULL

m=5

for(i in 1:m) {

mice.imp[[i]] <- complete(datami,action=i,include=FALSE)

}

out1 <- runMI(analyzeModel,data=mice.imp, chi = "all", ordered=paste0("y", 1:4), fun="sem")

On 03/31/2014 01:17 PM, Jeffrey Henry wrote:
> Dear all,

> should download to produce a marginal maximum likelihood (MML) estimator
> in a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA).

I'm not sure what you are asking for. Syntax? Nothing special, just
describe your model as usual. To use MML, simply add estimator="MML" to
the cfa/sem/lavaan call.

For example:

# create binary data
HS9 <-
HolzingerSwineford1939[,c("x1","x2","x3","x4","x5","x6","x7","x8","x9")]
HSbinary <- as.data.frame( lapply(HS9, cut, 2, labels=FALSE) )

# describe model (here a one-dimensional cfa)
model <- ' trait =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9 '

# fit model
fit <- cfa(model, data=HSbinary, ordered=names(HSbinary), std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,
estimator="MML")

# look at results
summary(fit)

Other R packages? Look at the 'mirt' package. Which is currently much,
much faster (using C++), but MML only.

References? Try anything with 'IRT'.

Some books:

van der Linden, W. J., & Hambleton, R. K. (Eds.). (1997). Handbook of
modern item response theory. New York, NY: Springer.

Hambleton, R.K., and Swaminathan, H. Item Response Theory: Principles
and Applications. Hingham, MA: Kluwer, Nijhoff, 1984.

Skrondal, A., & Rabe-Hesketh, S. (2004). Generalized latent variable
modeling: Multilevel, longitudinal, and structural equation models. CRC
Press.

Bartholomew, D. J., Knott, M., & Moustaki, I. (2011). Latent variable
models and factor analysis: a unified approach (Vol. 899). John Wiley &
Sons.

Yves.
